title: The sages were human
hook: the Talmud records its heroes' flaws and quarrels

segments.voice: Yesterday, the talmud laughs: a pun about builders, a bird on the line, a mouse with bread. Did you begin something with a little lightness? Day one thousand one hundred twenty-four.

A calf is being led to slaughter. It breaks away, runs to a great rabbi, and hides its head in the folds of his robe, crying. The rabbi is Rabbi Judah the Prince, the sage tradition credits with editing the Mishnah. He looks down at the frightened animal and says: go. For this you were created. And he lets them take it away. The Talmud tells this about one of its own heroes, plainly, and it doesn't stop there.
screen: `A CALF RUNS TO THE RABBI.` → `GO. FOR THIS YOU WERE CREATED.` → `THE TALMUD TELLS IT ON PURPOSE.`

segments.voice: Tractate Bava Metzia tells it plainly. Because he showed no compassion, suffering came upon Rabbi Judah, and stayed with him for years. Then one day his maid was sweeping the house and came upon some young weasels, and began to sweep them out. He stopped her. Let them be, he said, and quoted the Psalm: "His tender mercies are over all His works." And the Talmud says that because he showed compassion, the suffering left him. Notice what the book has done. It could have polished him into a statue. Instead it shows a giant in a cold moment, the cost of that moment, and the small act that turned him. And it isn't a lone story. The Talmud also tells how Rabban Gamliel, the head of the sages, was removed from leadership after he publicly shamed a colleague. The heroes misjudge, wound each other and change, right there on the page, in front of every student who will ever open it. Why would a tradition tell its children that their heroes failed? One answer: if the sages were perfect, nobody could follow them. A flawless teacher leaves you nothing to do but admire. A teacher who failed and turned leaves you a path. And the teaching keeps going past the teacher's flaw. Rabbi Judah's Mishnah is still studied, and so is the story of the calf and the weasels, side by side.
screen: `THE CALF HIDES IN HIS ROBE.` · `THE WEASELS: LET THEM BE.` · `HEROES WHO FAIL ON THE PAGE.` · `A FLAWED TEACHER LEAVES A PATH.` · then, large: `HIS TENDER MERCIES ARE OVER ALL HIS WORKS.`

segments.voice: Today's practice is to accept one hero's flaw. Settle, and breathe slowly. Bring to mind someone you look up to: a teacher, a parent, a public figure, a figure from scripture. Now let one of their real flaws come into view, one you already know about. Don't defend them, and don't throw them away. Hold both at once: what you admire, and where they fell short. Notice whether the admiration survives. Then, gently, let one of your own flaws stand next to theirs, and keep breathing. The bell holds the time.
The sages were human. The Talmud keeps its heroes' cold moments, quarrels and turnings on the page, so students can follow them, not only admire them. Today's word.
Your line: the sages were human. Today, when someone you admire lets you down, remember Rabbi Judah and the weasels: a flaw can be followed by a turning. Day one thousand one hundred twenty-four.

howItsDone: Students of the Talmud meet its sages' mistakes and quarrels in the text itself, and teachers often discuss what those stories teach about humility, compassion and repair.
